posts.title: Your Merchant Banker Knows SEBI. Does He Know Your Industry?
posts.excerpt: Filing for an IPO in India without a sector-specific advisor is how founders leave crores on the table.
posts.content:
India has over a million registered CAs, thousands of merchant bankers, and hundreds of investment advisory firms. So why do founders planning an IPO still end up working with someone who has never taken a company in their sector public before?

This is the expert discovery problem that nobody talks about openly. The professional exists. The credentials are real. But the match is wrong — and in IPO Advisory, a wrong match does not just cost you time. It costs you valuation, investor confidence, and sometimes the listing itself.

Here is what this looks like in practice. A Coimbatore-based textile manufacturer with ₹180 crore in revenue decides to go public on the NSE SME platform. Their CA refers them to a merchant banker he knows from a conference. The banker is competent — he has handled six IPOs. All six were in logistics and FMCG. He has never worked with a manufacturing business that carries high inventory, cyclical margins, and machinery depreciation as core financial features. The DRHP he drafts undersells the company's asset base. The valuation model does not adequately account for the sector's working capital cycle. Institutional investors flag it. The IPO underperforms its potential by a margin that the promoter family will feel for years.

The banker was not incompetent. He was the wrong expert for this specific need.

This is what makes expert discovery in India so structurally broken for complex, high-stakes problems. There is no reliable directory of who has done exactly what. Referrals are based on relationships, not track records. Google surfaces names with good SEO, not verified depth. LinkedIn shows credentials but not real-world outcomes. And by the time you realise the mismatch, you are already deep into a process that is expensive to unwind.

For IPO Advisory specifically, the gaps are sharper than most people realise. The advisor you need is not just someone who understands SEBI's ICDR regulations — everyone in the room does. What you actually need depends entirely on your situation. Are you a profitable SME going to BSE SME or NSE Emerge for the first time? You need someone who has navigated the SME IPO route specifically, understands how to position profitability for retail investors, and knows which registrars and market makers actually deliver. Are you a growth-stage company with complex ESOP structures and foreign shareholding? You need an advisor who has resolved exactly those complications in a DRHP before — not one who will figure it out on your file. Are you in pharma, agri, or deep manufacturing? You need someone who has built a credible industry narrative for institutional investors in your specific vertical, not a generalist who will borrow language from a software company's prospectus.

The difference between these profiles is enormous. And finding the right one through a referral network or a directory is, frankly, a matter of luck.

posts.title: The Nagpur Retailer Who Paid Twice for the Wrong Digital Advice
posts.excerpt: Digital transformation isn't just 'going online' — and the wrong consultant can cost you a year and a crore.
posts.content:
Rahul Deshmukh runs a mid-sized furniture retail chain out of Nagpur. Four showrooms, a warehouse, thirty-odd staff, and a business his father built over twenty-five years. In 2023, Rahul decided it was time to digitise — inventory management, a proper e-commerce channel, maybe some ERP integration. He'd watched competitors in Pune and Hyderabad make the shift and he knew he was falling behind.

He did what most business owners do. He asked around. A cousin referred him to a digital agency in Mumbai — a boutique firm that had built some good-looking websites and run performance marketing campaigns for D2C brands. They seemed credible. They had a deck. They had case studies. He signed a contract worth ₹14 lakh.

Six months later, Rahul had a website that looked reasonable and an inventory system that didn't talk to his billing software. The agency had no real experience with retail operations, supply chain workflows, or ERP architecture. They were marketers who had expanded their offerings because the market demanded it. When Rahul pushed back, they brought in a freelancer from Bangalore who had done some SAP work — but not in retail, not at this scale, and not with the specific point-of-sale systems Rahul used. The integration never worked properly. Rahul had spent fourteen months and burned most of his transformation budget before he admitted the project had failed.

This is not an unusual story. It plays out in Surat, in Coimbatore, in Ludhiana, in hundreds of businesses every year. The phrase gets attached to everything from a new website to an AI-powered supply chain overhaul. There are professionals in this country who have run digital transformation projects for retail chains with multi-city operations, who know exactly which ERP works at which scale, who understand the integration challenges between legacy POS systems and modern inventory platforms. The problem is that Rahul couldn't find one. His personal network didn't reach that far. The referral he got was well-intentioned but imprecise. LinkedIn searches returned generalists. posts.title: Your Startup Lawyer Knows Contracts — But Not Your ESOP Cliff

posts.title: Your Lawyer Knows Contracts. But Not This Contract Dispute.

The clause specified a seat of arbitration in Singapore with SIAC rules, a common feature in contracts with multinational distribution chains but easy to miss for a lawyer whose practice is rooted in domestic civil litigation. The lawyer did not flag the jurisdictional complexity early enough. He drafted arguments appropriate for a domestic dispute. The opposing counsel — a specialist in cross-border commercial arbitration — dismantled them.

posts.title: Your Digital Transformation Is Stalling. Here Is Why.
posts.excerpt: Most organisations don't fail at transformation because of technology — they fail because they trusted the wrong expert.
posts.content:
The boardroom approved the budget. The roadmap was ambitious. The vendor promised results in six months. Eighteen months later, your legacy systems still haven't migrated, your teams are running parallel workflows on spreadsheets, and the consultant who sold you the vision is three projects away and no longer returning calls at the same urgency.

This is not a technology failure. This is an expertise failure.

Digital transformation is one of the most consequential decisions a modern organisation will make — and one of the most dangerously misunderstood. It sits at the intersection of technology architecture, organisational change management, regulatory compliance, cybersecurity infrastructure, and financial planning. Yet most businesses approach it by hiring a generalist IT firm or trusting a referral from someone who went through a different transformation in a different industry five years ago.

The consequences are severe. Projects overrun by 40 to 70 percent. Customer-facing systems that go live with critical vulnerabilities. Teams that never adopt new platforms because the implementation ignored human behaviour. Data that gets migrated but never governed. And perhaps most damaging of all — leadership confidence that erodes quietly, month by month, until the transformation becomes the organisation's most expensive lesson.

Finding the right expert for digital transformation is genuinely hard. The domain is vast. A cloud migration specialist is not the same as a digital product strategist. A fintech automation expert operates in a fundamentally different paradigm than a healthcare systems integrator. An expert who transformed a 5,000-person enterprise may have no practical insight for a founder scaling from 50 to 500. Credentials on a CV rarely tell you whether someone has navigated regulatory constraints specific to your industry, managed vendor relationships under pressure, or led a transformation that survived leadership changes and budget cuts.

MahaYukti was built precisely for this gap. India's first private, multi-domain professional network, MahaYukti connects businesses, founders, and executives with verified, elite professionals across law, finance, technology, cybersecurity, medicine, and intelligence — professionals who are not available through a generic freelance marketplace or a consulting firm's rotating bench.

Consider a mid-sized financial services firm preparing to migrate its core banking operations to a cloud-native architecture. The stakes are existential — regulatory scrutiny from the RBI, zero tolerance for downtime, and a workforce that has operated the same system for over a decade. This firm does not need a generalist cloud consultant. It needs someone who has specifically navigated RBI compliance frameworks, understands the integration complexities of legacy core banking systems, and has managed change at an institutional scale. Through MahaYukti, the firm connects directly with a technology professional who has led exactly this kind of engagement — not as a junior team member, but as the architect of the outcome.

Or consider a D2C founder who has built a thriving brand on manual processes and third-party platforms, now facing the pressure of scaling. The systems that worked at ten orders a day are breaking at a thousand. Inventory management is a crisis. Customer data is fragmented across five tools. The founder needs a digital transformation expert who understands e-commerce architecture, ERP integration, and the speed constraints of a bootstrapped operation — not a consultant who will propose a two-year enterprise implementation roadmap. MahaYukti surfaces professionals who match not just the domain, but the context.

Or imagine a hospital group expanding across three states, attempting to unify patient records, billing systems, and diagnostic workflows under a single digital infrastructure. The intersection of healthcare regulation, data privacy under the DPDP Act, and clinical workflow design demands an expert who lives at that precise crossroads. On MahaYukti, that expert exists — and is accessible.
